content: The WHO Steering Group for the 2016 antenatal care (ANC) guidelines was responsible for drafting key recommendation questions using the PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome). They identified and invited experts to participate as guideline methodologists and members of the guideline development and external review groups. The Steering Group also supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis, organized technical consultations, and finalized the guideline document. In collaboration with WHO regional offices, they will oversee the dissemination of the updated recommendations. These experts, many of whom contributed to the 2016 ANC guideline’s nutrition recommendations, brought diverse expertise in research, guideline development, clinical policy, and ANC interventions. The group also included a patient/consumer representative. The GDG reviewed evidence, advised on its interpretation, and formulated the final recommendation during an online meeting held on December 4–5, 2019. They also reviewed and approved the final guideline document before its submission to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The External Review Group (ERG) was a geographically and gender-balanced team of four members, including technical experts and stakeholders with an interest in evidence-informed ANC. This group peer-reviewed a preliminary version of the guideline document to identify factual errors, assess language clarity, and address contextual issues and implementation implications. However, the ERG did not have the authority to alter recommendations formulated by the GDG. The systematic review team, led by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, updated the quantitative systematic review and facilitated collaboration between systematic review authors and guideline methodologists. Methodologists from Evidence-based Medicine Consultancy Ltd (UK) conducted additional analyses requested by the GDG, while experts from Centro Rosarino de Estudios Perinatales (Argentina) appraised quantitative evidence using the GRADE methodology. Qualitative evidence experts from the University of Central Lancashire (UK) systematically reviewed studies on women’s and healthcare professionals’ views on ANC and synthesized this evidence. Representatives from external organizations, including FIGO, ICM, UNFPA, USAID, UNICEF, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, were invited as observers to the final GDG meeting. These organizations, which have a history of collaboration with WHO, are potential implementers of the guideline. Observers did not participate in formulating recommendations. WHO required all external contributors to disclose any potential conflicts of interest (COI) through a standardized Declaration of Interest (DOI) form. The Steering Group reviewed these forms to assess the severity of any declared conflicts and determine their impact on the individual’s ability to make objective judgments. Findings from DOI statements were managed on a case-by-case basis, and experts with minor conflicts were required to declare them during GDG meetings. A summary of DOI statements and their management is included in Annex 2. The priority question and outcomes for the updated recommendation were aligned with the 2016 ANC guideline. These were informed by a scoping exercise of existing clinical practice guidelines and systematic reviews, as well as a WHO-commissioned qualitative review of what women want during pregnancy. The findings emphasized the importance of a positive pregnancy experience, defined as maintaining physical and sociocultural normality, ensuring a healthy pregnancy and baby, transitioning effectively to positive labor and birth, and achieving positive motherhood. This overarching principle guided the ANC guideline recommendations. Evidence supporting the recommendation was derived from updated Cochrane systematic reviews and additional analyses conducted by methodologists. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the certainty of quantitative evidence, which was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on established criteria. Qualitative evidence was appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which evaluates methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The GDG reviewed the evidence summary during an online meeting on December 4–5, 2019, and made judgments on the intervention’s impact based on six criteria: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The intervention could be recommended, not recommended, or recommended in specific contexts, such as rigorous research or targeted monitoring and evaluation. The guideline document was drafted by the WHO Steering Group, reviewed by participants and the ERG, and revised based on their input. Final modifications were limited to correcting factual errors and improving clarity. The document was then submitted for executive clearance following WHO publication procedures. The evidence and recommendation on antenatal multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS) were detailed in the guideline. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showed a 12% reduction in low birth weight with MMS compared to iron and folic acid (IFA) supplements. However, subgroup analyses suggested that IFA supplements with 60 mg of iron might be associated with lower neonatal mortality than MMS. The GDG noted that the clinical significance of these findings was difficult to interpret, as the reduction in low birth weight included both preterm births and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) births, for which no difference was observed between MMS and IFA. The GDG rated the certainty of evidence for maternal anemia, low birth weight, and stillbirth as high; for SGA, preterm birth, perinatal mortality, and neonatal mortality as moderate; and for cesarean section, maternal mortality, and congenital anomalies as low. The recommendation emphasized the need for further research, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, sustainability, equity, and cost-effectiveness of MMS programs.
